item.title: [PELJ] Unilateral Reduction of Employees' Salaries in the Context of COVID-19 Pandemic: Macsteel Service Centres SA (Pty) Ltd v National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa (NUMSA) 2020 8 BLLR 772 (LC)
item.dc:creator: Chillion H Ncube
item.description: In Macsteel Service Centres SA (Pty) Ltd v National Union of Metal Workers of South Africa (NUMSA) 2020 8 BLLR 772 (LC), the Labour Court handed down a judgment relating to a salary cut imposed by an employer due to COVID-19 and lockdown. The case came before the Labour Court as an urgent application by Macsteel ("employer") to interdict an unprotected strike by NUMSA. The judgment specifically dealt with the issue as to whether a unilateral reduction of salaries imposed by the employer for the months of May, June and July 2020 was unlawful as contemplated in sections 64(4) and (5) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995. The Labour Court made a detailed analysis of Macsteel's operations and concluded that where employees had tendered services, they are entitled to full remuneration. The court found that the 20% salary reduction was unlawful as it amounted to a unilateral change to employees' conditions of employment. The Macsteel judgment is welcomed and further confirms the correct approach in law, that in instances where it is legally impermissible for employees to perform their duties, the employer is entitled to enforce the "no work, no pay" principle based on the impossibility of performance by both parties. The judgment affirmed the application of the "no work, no pay" principle, specifically that employees who were unable to work during the COVID-19 lockdown were not entitled to their salaries.

item.title: [PELJ] Interrogating the Practice of Lawful Interception of Communications and the Right to Privacy in Nigeria and South Africa
item.dc:creator: David T Eyongndi, Garvin U Oyibodoro, Onyinye Ucheagwu-Okoye, Ademola O Ojekunle, Chidimma S Nwakoby, Hilary Nwaechefu
item.description: Section 37 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (CFRN 1999) guarantees the right to privacy. This right is recognised by international legal frameworks like the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 1966 and, by expansive interpretation, the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, 1981. However, section 45 of the CFRN 1999 empowers the legislature to make laws that derogate from specific rights under Chapter IV thereof, and section 37 is one of the derogable rights. Consequently the Nigerian Communications Act, 2003 (NCA 2003), which established the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) with powers to make regulations, was enacted. Pursuant to the NCA 2003 the NCC made the Lawful Interception of Communications Regulations, 2019 (LICR 2019), permitting security agencies to intercept communications in furtherance of national security, crime prevention/investigation, safeguarding the economic well-being of Nigerians, etc. As in Nigeria, the right to privacy is guaranteed in South Africa, but the Regulation of Interception of Communications and Provision of Communication-Related Information Act 70 of 2002 (RICA 2002) permits the interception of communication, with reasonable guardrails provided. The issues arising from this practice are the following. Is the interception of communication under the LICR 2019 and RICA 2002 a necessity or an intrusion into the right of privacy? How can the right to privacy be safeguarded against this practice? And what lessons can Nigeria learn from the South African experience on the interception of communication? This article adopts a comparative method, relying on primary and secondary data in interrogating these issues, gleaning from the practice in South Africa. It finds that the implementation of the LICR 2019 is susceptible to abuse by the implementers, unlike the RICA 2002, which contains guardrails; that the sanctions prescribed for violation by implementers are incapable of instilling deterrence, and that there is a need to create a symbiotic co-existence between the right to privacy and the LICR 2019. It recommends the amendment of the LICR 2019 by the imposition of stiffer sanctions for breach, and the public enlightenment of security agencies towards lawful implementation.

item.title: [CILSA] Food Security as a Consideration in Anti-Dumping Investigations Conducted by the International Trade Administration Commission: Lessons for South Africa from the European Commission
item.dc:creator: Jeanette Visagie, Marucia Fick
item.description: Following the decision by the South African Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition to suspend anti-dumping duties in the International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC) Chicken Meat Dumping Investigation case, and the subsequent outbreak of disease amongst poultry, this article analyses the need to consider food security as part of the ‘public interest’ during anti-dumping investigations relating to essential food products. ITAC and the Minister of Trade are mandated, in terms of the relevant legal framework, to consider public interest as an additional fourth requirement on an ad hoc basis during anti-dumping investigations that may impact food security in South Africa and other Southern African Customs Union countries. Accessibility and availability elements of food security are affected by factors such as the type of product and whether it is an essential food, possible supply constraints impacting local food production, the prevalence or risk of disease outbreak, and the likelihood that price increases following the imposition of anti-dumping duties will be passed on to the end consumer. ITAC should consider these factors during anti-dumping investigations in a manner similar to the European Union’s consideration of the Union interest, ultimately assisting the Minister of Trade in making a decision regarding the imposition of anti-dumping duties in matters related to essential food products. If such an approach is adopted, it would be in line with the government’s obligation and responsibility to protect, promote and fulfil the right to access to sufficient food.

item.title: [SAPL] WTO Safeguards in Africa: Limited Use, Compliance Challenges and Capacity Constraints
item.dc:creator: Gustav Brink
item.description: Safeguards are one of three World Trade Organization (WTO)-sanctioned trade remedies that countries may use to protect their domestic industries against various forms of increased international competition. However, few African countries make use of the instrument, with only Egypt, Madagascar, Morocco and South Africa as active users, while three more countries have each conducted a single safeguard investigation. There are some WTO inconsistencies in the way each of these countries conduct safeguard investigations, but nothing that cannot be addressed without too much effort. Other African countries, especially the more industrialised countries such as Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania, should finalise their safeguards legislation and request technical assistance from the WTO and the African countries actively using the instrument to rapidly upskill to allow themselves to use the instrument. Safeguards can be instrumental in protecting domestic industries against increased imports and allow them the opportunity to adjust to such increased competition, thereby enabling African countries to participate more fully in international trade and beneficiate raw materials domestically, all of which could contribute to Africa’s economic growth.

item.title: [SAPL] Educational Standards, Qualifications and Competency Frameworks for Councillors in South African Municipalities—A Constitutional Need
item.dc:creator: Nonhlanhla Ngcobo
item.description: The Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (CoGTA) is currently reviewing the 1998 White Paper on Local Government, marking the beginning of a new era for a sphere whose constitutional and legislative powers have significantly contributed to the development of local communities. Despite this recognition, local government continues to face persistent challenges, including deficiencies in administrative governance, service delivery backlogs, infrastructure constraints, and both financial and structural limitations. However, the review of the White Paper fails to acknowledge that many of these challenges can be significantly attributed to the low literacy levels of councillors—the key decision-makers in municipalities—among other factors. This omission persists despite the minister’s public admission that more than 300 councillors in the KwaZulu-Natal Province are unable to read or write. This article argues that the absence of minimum educational, expertise and competency requirements for councillors may undermine the effective implementation of the proposed reforms, especially given the increasing complexity of political, financial and administrative tasks and decision-making within the local government sphere. The article undertakes a critical analysis of political rights and principles enshrined in the Constitution in the context of the dysfunctional local government in South Africa, and in response, offers a carefully crafted councillor competency capacity development framework that does not encroach on the relevant constitutional guarantees.

item.title: [CILSA] Eligibility of Victims of International Crimes for Reparations before the International Criminal Court: A Critique
item.dc:creator: Bongani M Dlamini, Linda Mushoriwa
item.description: The adoption of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court on 17 July 1998 and the establishment of the International Criminal Court (ICC or the Court) on 2 July 2002 marked a significant turn for international criminal justice. Notably, the Court established a platform for bringing justice to victims of international crimes, whilst putting the victims at the centre of proceedings. One way in which this is evident is the framework for awarding reparations to victims of the core crimes of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. This not only serves to acknowledge the victims’ pain and suffering but also to remedy the harm they have suffered. The Court’s mandate to award reparations to victims of international crimes is provided for in Article 75 of the Rome Statute. The purpose of this article is to examine the Court’s reparations regime with respect to the eligibility of victims to receive reparations as provided for in the Rome Statute, and as seen through the lens of the Court’s jurisprudence on this subject. The article asserts that whilst the reparations regime is an innovative way to deliver justice to victims of atrocities, its effectiveness remains subject to debate due to challenges associated with the interpretation of the meaning of ‘victims’ for purposes of reparations, and the eligibility criteria for victims to be awarded reparations. It concludes that the Court must consider amending its procedural laws to allow flexibility and place more prominence on the content of reparations delivered in individual cases.

item.title: [CILSA] Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation in Zimbabwe: Lessons from South Africa
item.dc:creator: Basutu S Makwaiba
item.description: The purpose of this article is to critically review the judicial approach to delegated legislation in Zimbabwe. One of the firmly entrenched principles in constitutional law is that legislative power cannot be delegated. The limitation on the legislature’s delegation of its primary law-making powers is based on the doctrine of non-delegation. The non-delegation doctrine commands that the legislature alone exercise law-making power. This article examines the extent to which the Zimbabwean courts have enforced the non-delegation doctrine when reviewing executive law-making under the Presidential Powers (Temporary Measures) Act. The courts have held that the Act is constitutional even though it assigns Parliament’s primary law-making to the executive. The article used a doctrinal research methodology to analyse existing primary and secondary sources. It also included a desk review, which employed a comparative methodology. The comparative analysis focused on South Africa, selected for its judiciary’s ability to exert stronger oversight over the delegation of legislative authority to the executive. The South African courts have defined the limits to which legislative powers may be delegated distinguishing between delegation to make subordinate legislation and assigning primary law-making power to another body. This article aims to contribute to the existing literature on the nature and extent of constitutional limitations on the delegation of legislative powers. There is a conspicuous dearth of scholarly literature examining judicial oversight of delegated legislation in Zimbabwe, and this study addresses that gap.

item.title: [PELJ] Editorial: Legal-Technical Governance and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in Africa
item.dc:creator: Chijioke Okorie, Vukosi Marivate
item.description: This editorial introduces the special issue on the legal-technical governance and regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) in Africa, the product of a project launched by the Data Science Law Lab in collaboration with the Data Science for Social Impact research group at the University of Pretoria. It situates the five peer-reviewed contributions within a legal-technical approach to AI governance: a transdisciplinary approach in which the legal and the technical are fused to add nuance to regulatory forms and practices and to close the legal-technical gap in AI governance and regulation. The contributions move from conceptual foundations, where legal-technical governance is advanced as an analytical framework, through continental norm-making on the transition from African Union soft law to an AI treaty and national policy design on intellectual property in African AI strategies, to the operation of AI systems in practice, addressing the algorithmic sovereignty gap in AI-enabled surveillance in South Africa and Nigeria and the legal status of predictive policing in the fight against cybercrime in Nigeria.

item.title: [Obiter] ESTA Occupiers and the Construction of Buildings and Homesteads on Farmland: Addressing Critical Issues in Light of Prinsloo NO v Ngcongwane [2023] ZALCC 22 and Basfour 3327 (Pty) Ltd v Thwala (Leave to Appeal) [2023] ZALCC 28
item.dc:creator: Lerato Rudolph Ngwenyama
item.description: The purpose of the Extension of Security of Tenure Act (62 of 1997) (ESTA) is to enhance and promote the ideal of long-term security of tenure for occupiers of land on an equitable basis, promote land-tenure reform as a means of redressing the results of past discrimination and facilitate land-tenure justice. The history of land dispossession and labour tenancy is important to this context and connects with the purpose of ESTA. To fulfil the purpose of ESTA as contemplated in the Preamble, the objects of ESTA are, among others, to afford certain rights and duties to persons who reside on land that they do not own.

item.title: [CILSA] Lawyers are Safe from the AI Invasion—For Now! A Brief Consideration of the Use of Artificially Generated Tools in Legal Research in SA and the US
item.dc:creator: Ciresh Singh, Menelisi Ncube
item.description: A legal maxim holds that ‘it is not knowing all the law that counts but knowing where to find the law that makes a good lawyer a great lawyer,’ highlighting the importance of legal research. While technology and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed research and drafting, they are prone to errors, including fabricated authorities. Courts, especially in the United States (US), have sanctioned misuse and South African courts have raised concerns, though no regulations yet exist. This paper examines AI use in legal research by undertaking a detailed analysis of the recent case law, in the US and South Africa, that has considered this topic. This paper will be divided into five parts: Part 1 serves as an introduction and overview of the topic; Part 2 briefly considers some of the AI tools currently available and their possible application in legal practice; Part 3 investigates how some AI tools have been used in the US; Part 4 considers the use of AI tools in the South African legal system; and Part 5 serves as a conclusion and provides some key recommendations in this area. It is hoped that this discussion will bring to light the need for AI regulation and, possibly, the prompt implementation of guidelines and rules to regulate its use not only in legal practice, but also in society. The article draws on both primary and secondary materials and employs a qualitative desktop research method. This article calls for, inter alia, concerted efforts by the legislature and other relevant stakeholders to comprehensively regulate the use of AI by legal practitioners when conducting legal research in order to retain the integrity of the South African legal profession.

item.title: [Obiter] SCA Provides Clarity on the Requirements Needed for the Court to Grant Remedial Action for Oppressive and Unfair Conduct in Terms of Section 163 of the Companies Act 71 of 2008 - Parry v Dunn-Blatch [2024] ZASCA 19
item.dc:creator: Darren Subramanien, Dehal Jivan, Suhail Ebrahim
item.description: The “oppression remedy”, while having arguably undergone substantial legislative development over time, has long been a contentious issue for South African courts. The use of this remedy allows shareholders or directors to challenge, and seek relief from, certain acts or omissions they believe are oppressive or unfairly prejudicial, or that unfairly disregard their interests. In Parry v Dunn-Blatch ([2024] ZASCA 19), the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) had to consider whether the act or omission envisaged in section 163(1) of the Companies Act 71 of 2008 (the 2008 Act) had taken place as alleged by the applicant. The decision of the SCA in Parry v Dunn-Blatch (supra) is important as the court provided much-needed clarity as to what will be required by an applicant who wishes to bring a successful application for use of the remedy found in section 163 of the 2008 Act.

item.title: [Obiter] Competition Law as a Catalyst for Access to Education: A Review of a Drive against Anti-Competitive Practices in the Procurement of School Uniforms by the Competition Commission of South Africa
item.dc:creator: Sandiso Mbulawa
item.description: Exclusive agreements and high prices in some markets can harm competition, competitors, and consumers and may also affect the enjoyment of constitutionally protected rights. Some practices impinge on aspects of citizens’ fundamental rights, such as the right of access to education. In response to complaints from parents regarding anti-competitive practices involving schools, suppliers and/or manufacturers, the Competition Commission has undertaken a series of interventions to enhance competition in the procurement of school uniforms and other related materials. The initiative was aimed at promoting and balancing increasing competition in school-uniform procurement and to provide parents with more choices to ensure that they are not compelled to purchase school uniforms exclusively from selected suppliers. The initiative not only achieved market competitiveness, but, to a certain extent, it also secured the constitutional right to access to education. Therefore, the article examines the effectiveness of the Competition Commission’s interventions on the procurement of school uniforms and showcases the role the agency played in promoting access to education.

item.title: [Obiter] Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 3)
item.dc:creator: Jan-Louis van Tonder
item.description: Sections 4(1)(a) and (b) of the Competition Act 89 of 1998 reflect the distinction in competition law between horizontal restrictive practices that may be evaluated either through a “rule of reason” analysis or treated as automatically unlawful under a “per se” approach. Section 4(1)(a) contemplates a “rule of reason” analysis in terms of which the anti-competitive effects of the conduct in issue must be proved and, even if such effects are demonstrated, they are susceptible to justification on technological, efficiency or pro-competitive grounds. By contrast, where the impugned conduct involves any of the restrictive horizontal practices listed in section 4(1)(b), namely, price-fixing, market division or collusive tendering, it is prohibited “per se” in that the anti-competitive effect thereof is presumed and cannot be justified on technological, efficiency or pro-competitive grounds. As is the case with bona fide agreements that are embarked upon by competitors for a legitimate purpose, commercially reasonable ancillary restraints, even when concluded between competitors, ought not to be treated as automatically infringing section 4(1)(b) without further enquiry. For these purposes, the Competition Appeal Court (CAC) in Dawn Consolidated Holdings (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission (Dawn) has developed a well-refined test to assess whether a restraint of trade within a broader agreement, such as a joint venture, falls within the scope of the prohibitions enacted by section 4(1)(b) of the Competition Act. Part 1 critically reviews the applicable South African framework and principles relevant to characterisation as developed in American Natural Soda Ash Corporation v Competition Commission and Competition Commission v South African Breweries Ltd and assesses the approach to whether conduct is anti-competitive by object or effect under article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (EU). Part 2 builds on Part 1 by reviewing and assessing key facets of characterisation that have further emerged from notable cases such as Aranda Textile Mills (Pty) Ltd v The Competition Commission of South Africa, Tourvest Holdings (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission, Competition Commission of South Africa v Irwin & Johnson, and Competition Commission v Waco Africa (Pty) Ltd. Part 3 reviews and assesses the approach relevant to characterisation of ancillary restraints of trade as developed by the CAC in Dawn. Pursuant to section 1(3) of the Competition Act, appropriate foreign and international law may be considered when interpreting or applying the Competition Act. This is complementary to section 1(2)(a), which directs that the Competition Act must be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with the Constitution and that gives effect to the purposes set out in section 2. In light hereof, this article also considers the approaches in the United Kingdom, the EU and the United States. (Van Tonder “Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 1)” 2025 46(4) Obiter 872–886; Van Tonder “Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 2)” 2026 47(1) Obiter 1–14)

item.title: [Obiter] Foreclosure of Primary Home Mortgages in Namibia: Towards Efficient Judicial Oversight
item.dc:creator: PC Nhekairo, NV Asheela-Shikalepo
item.description: Mortgage foreclosures represent a significant and contentious issue, particularly when they pertain to individuals’ primary homes. Foreclosure inherently creates a conflict between two opposing interests: the mortgagee’s entitlement to enforce their security and the imperative to alleviate the severe repercussions of displacing the mortgagor and their family, which could lead to homelessness. In Namibia, the relevance of mortgage foreclosure concerning primary homes is exacerbated by a persistent housing crisis; thus, displacing a mortgagor and their family contributes to the alarming statistic that about 25 per cent of the population lacks access to adequate housing. The interplay of interests among the mortgagor, the mortgagee and external entities such as the government necessitates a careful balancing exercise in the enforcement of mortgage foreclosures. The execution of foreclosures on primary homes in Namibia is primarily governed by rule 108 of the High Court Rules, which mandates judicial oversight prior to declaring primary homes specially executable. This article contends that the existing regulatory framework in Namibia does not adequately reconcile the competing interests associated with the foreclosure of primary homes. Based on the results of a comparative analysis, this article ultimately proposes the promulgation of a comprehensive foreclosure regulatory framework.

item.title: [Obiter] The Constitutional and Legislative Powers of Local Authorities in South Africa: The Applicability of an Ocean Accounts Framework as an Ocean-Governance Instrument
item.dc:creator: Hendrik J Van As
item.description:
This research examines the Ocean Accounts Framework (OAF) as an instrument for ocean governance and policy development by South African local authorities. The Constitution imposes sustainable developmental duties on municipalities, requiring them to budget and plan in a way that prioritises basic community needs and promotes social and economic development. With their funding primarily coming from property rates, service surcharges and payments from national government, municipalities are responsible for local economic and infrastructure development, promoting a safe and healthy environment, and service delivery.

Coastal management is the shared responsibility of all three branches of government and frequently overlaps. South Africa adopted the National Development Plan (NDP) to promote economic growth and address the triple challenge of inequality, unemployment and poverty. Operation Phakisa prioritises marine transport, offshore oil and gas, aquaculture and marine protection services. 

This article examines the relationship between the OAF and the legislative and policy instruments that guide coastal and ocean governance in South Africa’s local government sphere. As part of a community of practice (CoP), the research assesses the applicability of the OAF in South Africa and the Western Indian Ocean (WIO), with a focus on the legal context in which the OAF is to be used. It investigates the constitutional and legislative powers and functions of local authorities that are relevant to the blue economy and the extent to which municipalities exercise these powers and functions. It also assesses the OAF’s potential to evaluate food security and sustainability risks for local populations, and whether local authorities can legislate against marine-resource crimes to augment national legislation. Finally, the study argues that using the OAF to measure ocean value for municipal development could boost funding and help local authorities meet the requirements set by the Constitution, the NDP and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Local authorities should realise the importance of the ocean and its living resources and use a credible valuation tool to exercise their legislative powers.

item.title: [JJS] Comparative analysis of child consent laws in health care decisions in South Africa, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada
item.dc:creator: Frans Mahlobogwane
item.description: Over the last few decades, laws worldwide have increasingly evolved to allow minors to, inter alia, consent to their own health care services. These laws, when compared, are oftentimes inconsistent with one another, with variations between countries as regards the minimum age of consent, the classes of minors that may consent, and the context within which consent may be considered valid. Furthermore, these laws have altered the discourse on health care access as it relates to children, specifically because health care providers must adhere to minor consent laws when addressing the needs of adolescent patients. Considering the above it is crucial, in a comparative and medico legal context, to understand whether and how minors may consent on their own to receive various types of health care services. This paper reflects on the way in which various jurisdictions, including South Africa, have treated the issue of child consent when it comes to health care decisions and services. It provides a brief overview of the laws governing minors’ capacity to consent to health care, considering the complexity of the concept of evolving legal standing and the process of children’s participation in the health care environment. Comparing South Africa with the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada reveals distinct legal philosophies, specifically the shift from fixed-age limits to “competence-based” assessments. Consequently, the paper recommends that South Africa would do well to develop guiding principles for assessing a child’s decision-making capacity in line with international practices.

item.title: [JJS] Contra non valentem in South Africa: A transformative evaluation of whether the death of a land owner should delay the completion of acquisitive prescription∗
item.dc:creator: Ernst Marais
item.description: The Gauteng Local Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, recently had to decide a vexing legal question, namely whether the law delays (or postpones) the running of acquisitive prescription (“prescription”) under the contra non valentem agere non currit praescriptio (prescription does not run against those who cannot assert their rights) maxim if a landowner passed away. If so, prescription would be postponed until the beneficiaries appointed an executor to the deceased estate. The court answered this question affirmatively by holding that no one can stop (or interrupt) the running of prescription prior to the appointment of an executor, that prescription promotes legal certainty and not the personal interest of the possessor, and that the possessor’s acquiring ownership in a case like the present could possibly entail an arbitrary deprivation of the deceased owner’s property. This paper investigates the legal question from the perspective of South African private law doctrine, comparative law, legal theory, and in terms of the property and housing clauses in the Constitution. My conclusions are that (i) beneficiaries have standing to interrupt prescription, (ii) foreign law favours the promotion of legal certainty over the protection of an (incapacitated) owner when the prescription period is long, (iii) postponing prescription in a case like Katha v Pillay discourages beneficiaries from appointing an executor timeously, thereby causing further neglect of the land (and prolonging the uncertainty of its legal status), (iv) recognising too many grounds of postponement would undermine the legal certainty rationale in countries with negative registration systems (like South Africa), (v) moral reasons indicate that a possessor’s long-existing home interest in land is worthy of protection, and (vi) that vesting ownership of land in such a possessor would amount to a transformative outcome, despite the owner’s death (provided she satisfies the other prescription requirements as well). These conclusions draw the court’s ruling on the postponement matter into question.

item.title: [JJS] Piercing the trust veil at divorce: A constitutionally compliant common law approach to rendering trust assets liable to attachment in satisfaction of matrimonial property claims – Part One
item.dc:creator: Bradley Smith
item.description: Remedial action following a court’s decision to “pierce the veil” of an abused trust at divorce typically involves adding a trust’s asset value for the purposes of calculating the errant spouse’s matrimonial property liability. Although the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) has mooted the possibility of further action via a declaration that trust assets are to be “used … to satisfy” a patrimonial claim, this avenue remains unexplored. It has, however, recently come to light that in the 2020 matter of LW v CW, the Western Cape High Court ordered the transfer of an abused trust’s assets “[i]n the event of [the errant spouse] holding insufficient assets in his personal capacity to satisfy [the other spouse’s] accrual claim.” This notwithstanding, in 2023 the South African Law Reform Commission (SALRC) proposed an amendment to the Divorce Act 70 of 1979 that would empower a court to distribute trust property to a spouse whose matrimonial property entitlement has been frustrated by means of a trust. Part One of this contribution argues that while the ability to access trust assets by judicial intervention is essential to affording effective relief to such spouses, statutory reform is unnecessary. This is because the common law provides a viable alternative, by instead permitting trust assets to be attached, if necessary, to satisfy a matrimonial property debt. This assertion is based on answering what this contribution identifies as the core “deprivation question”, namely whether the common law principles pertaining to piercing the corporate veil permit a company to be deprived of its assets to satisfy a debt that is not its own, but rather that of a related individual (such as a shareholder) owed to a third party. An analysis of pre-constitutional case law – as the only available case law on point – permits the distillation of several fundamental precepts that permit a positive answer to this question. The discussion then moves to the trust/divorce law context, where the principles which have become established – as well as those that can be deduced – from leading SCA case law in respect of a court’s ability to pierce the veil of an abused trust at divorce and their potential relevance to the deprivation question are considered. Building on these, Part One concludes with preliminary insights into the theoretical underpinnings of rendering trust property liable to attachment at divorce. Part Two will expand on these underpinnings by considering the constitutional ramifications of the deprivation question. Ultimately, this comprehensive analysis will achieve the main aim of this contribution, which is to conceptualise a constitutionally compliant approach to be followed by aggrieved spouses who seek the potential attachment of trust assets where necessary. To this end, an incremental development of the common law is required. Part Two will conclude by comparing this approach to the one taken in LW v CW with a view to securing a more satisfactory legal position.

item.title: [JJS] The coordinated role and functions of international finance institutes in mitigating economic crime and fostering financial stability: A multi-dimensional South African analysis
item.dc:creator: Eureka Eulogy Ndhlovu
item.description: Within South Africa’s evolving financial regulatory landscape, global financial institutions play an increasingly critical role in shaping anti-economic crime strategies and fostering financial stability. This paper undertakes a multi-dimensional analysis of the coordinated and individual contributions of the Institute of International Finance (IIF), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the World Economic Forum (WEF), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank (WB), the World Trade Organization (WTO), the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) in mitigating economic crime. While the discussion draws on global policy frameworks and innovation models, it remains rooted in the South African context , examining national legal instruments, regulatory sandboxes, and fintech developments. Case studies from South Africa and peer jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom, Nigeria, and Singapore offer comparative insight into sandbox mechanisms. Ultimately, the paper evaluates how international institutions influence domestic frameworks and provides South Africa-focused recommendations for regulatory enhancement.

item.title: [JJS] Inferior by law –Ethnographic results in the Limpopo province of the interaction between traditional justice and the state law as encompassed by the Traditional Courts Act
item.dc:creator: Lesetja Monyamane
item.description: South African jurisprudence attempts to employ a dual trajectory of law that includes customary law. However, this duality has been – and regrettably remains – faulty in that it has never properly accounted for the perversion caused to the system of customary law by the now repealed Black Administration Act 38 of 1927. Despite being repealed, its disregard of Native legal imagination and the cultural location of customary law remain largely unaccounted for in South Africa. The paper finds it edifying that this disregard of Native legal capital and imagination has been furthered by the provisions of the Traditional Courts Act 9 of 2022. It is the further contention of the author that the Traditional Courts Act attempts to project traditional justice as an unsophisticated form of justice which is inferior to the state law and its other justice operatives. It is argued below that the Act perpetuates and sustains this supposed inferiority of customary law by intentionally excluding the true legal imagination and experiences of the Natives in determining their legal issues. The paper furthermore interrogates this marginalisation through an ethnographic inquiry conducted in the Limpopo Province, South Africa. The ethnographic data demonstrates a rich tapestry of traditional justice that is not only responsive but is indeed multifaceted. In essence, it is argued here, the Traditional Courts Act is a new attempt underlying the insistence by the state law to undermine customary law and, by extension, traditional justice.

item.title: [JJS] Transformation through the lens of South Africa’s Competition Act 89 of 1998
item.dc:creator: Tinashe Kondo
item.description: In this paper, I examine how and whether transformation can be achieved through South Africa’s Competition Act 89 of 1998. This issue is important due to the lack of studies exploring the linkages between transformation and competition law, particularly after the enactment of the Competition Amendment Act 18 of 2018. The inclusion of transformation objectives in the Competition Act 89 of 1998 (the Act/ Competition Act), as amended, has been a subject of debate, with some arguing that the primary goal of competition law should be economic efficiency and that transformation goals may conflict with this mandate. However, I contend that there is a theoretical foundation for incorporating transformation issues into the Competition Act 89 of 1998, supported by both economic and legal theory. I observe that transformation is a policy demand arising from South Africa’s competition policy. The paper furthermore explores how transformation has been integrated into the Act, illustrating that it is no longer merely an aspiration in competition law but is now embedded in various provisions beyond merger regulation and the Act’s stated purpose. Consequently, transformation has become a key consideration in the Act’s implementation and enforcement. My main argument in the paper is that transformation is not merely an economic consideration, but a legal imperative rooted in South Africa’s constitutional values and historical injustices. I recommend that legislators explore ways to better promote other transformation goals such as: advancing employment and improving the social and economic welfare of South Africa within the framework of the Act; considering ways to concretise the centrality of constitutional and human rights objectives within the Act; and including constitutional values as interpretive aids in the Act. In relation to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and businesses owned by historically disadvantaged persons (HDPs), I make the case that there be ways developed to quantify the harm to them as well as monitor the digital markets more closely for harm to these entities. Finally, I encourage competition authorities to examine the possible role and impact of other principles and values, such as ubuntu, within competition law.

item.title: [CILSA] Denationalisation and Statelessness: A Comparative Analysis of the Congolese, Eritrean, Ethiopian, and Sudanese Nationality Laws
item.dc:creator: Makda Gebru Hayle, Abdu Mohamedali Osman
item.description: This article examines the role of nationality laws in mitigating or aggravating statelessness, focusing on four African states characterised by high emigration rates: Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Ethiopia and Eritrea. It identifies the rejection of dual nationality and the proliferation of grounds for nationality revocation as primary drivers of statelessness, arguing that possessing additional nationalities often serves as the central justification for denationalisation. Moreover, through a comparative analysis of the selected nationality laws, the study highlights how some of the selected countries simultaneously benefit from their diasporas while refusing to formally allow the possession of dual nationalities. Methodologically, the article engages with primary sources, including national laws and international conventions, supplemented by secondary materials such as scholarly works on denationalisation and statelessness, official reports, and digital archives. It systematically evaluates divergences and parallels in revocation provisions across the selected countries, revealing contradictions between legal texts and their implementation. The study concludes with targeted legislative recommendations: Sudan, while permitting dual citizenship, must address discriminatory provisions affecting South Sudanese communities and tighten some of the grounds for the revocation of nationality. The DRC and Ethiopia should formally recognise dual nationality to respond to their realities and embrace the inevitable shift in this direction. Lastly, Eritrea’s outdated nationality law requires reform to align the practice with the law and introduce rules governing renationalisation and dual nationality and to tighten the grounds for the revocation of nationality. Collectively, these reforms would advance compliance with international law and reduce risks of statelessness.

item.title: [CILSA] Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Combat Crypto Money Laundering: A Regulatory Perspective
item.dc:creator: Parele Shamase
item.description: The emergence of multiple variations of crypto assets has the potential to enhance traditional monetary systems, reduce transaction costs, bolster data protection and promote financial inclusion. However, unique crypto features have also opened a modus operandi for cyberlaundering and weakened traditional anti-money laundering (AML) regulations. Malicious actors exploit the increased quasi-anonymity, cross-jurisdictional reach and decentralisation of crypto assets to facilitate money laundering. In 2022, crypto-asset service providers were declared accountable institutions in order to bring crypto assets under money laundering regulation and supervision in accordance with the Financial Intelligence Centre Act 38 of 2001. However, the current AML measures lack an innovative and forensic analysis angle to combat complex crypto money laundering strategies. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies can transform the execution of AML compliance in the crypto economy with enormous speed and greater efficiency. However, innovative technologies can also reinforce human bias, undermine data protection and cause operational challenges for financial institutions. Therefore, the strategic use of AI in AML control must balance sophisticated financial crime control initiatives with competing ethical and policy considerations to promote the sustainable development of the crypto ecosystem. This article examines the principles-based integration of AI-driven mitigation and control typologies to enhance financial security in the crypto medium. It investigates how AI-driven mitigation strategies can thrive in criminogenic crypto finance under legal safeguards of a structured and normative regulatory environment.

item.title: [JLSD] Flipping the Switch to a Green(er) Rural Economy in South Africa: Securing Community-Private Partnerships in the Renewable Energy Context
item.dc:creator: Tina Kotzé
item.description: The renewable energy sector is pivotal in the global transition to a low-carbon, climate resilient economy. Yet in South Africa, despite strong policy commitments to a just energy transition, rural communities continue to experience energy poverty and limited ownership or participation in renewable energy developments. A community-private partnership (CPP) is a collaborative model in which communities and private developers jointly own, govern, or benefit from renewable energy projects, enabling shared decision-making and equitable local benefit-sharing. This article, therefore, examines how CPPs can serve as a transformative model to secure rural livelihoods, enhance community agency, and address historical marginalisation. I draw on an interdisciplinary literature review, doctrinal legal analysis, and selected case studies to examine 1) the structural factors that limit meaningful community participation; 2) the archetypes of CPPs; and 3) the extent to which CPPs can be aligned with the International Renewable Energy Agency’s (IRENA) criteria for community ownership. I argue that CPPs aimed at shared ownership, supported by democratic governance and equitable benefit-sharing, offers a pragmatic and socially just pathway for South Africa’s emerging green economy.

item.title: [JLSD] Human Labour: A Commodity to Be Bought and Sold
item.dc:creator: Fanelesibonge Craig Mabaso
item.description: The question of whether human labour is a commodity to be bought and sold has been addressed in some spheres of academia but is yet to be addressed properly within the perspective of labour law. In this article I will answer this question through an examination of the theoretical arguments on the one hand and practical legal arguments on the other. The more traditional approach to the question, which takes the form of the practical legal perspective, concludes that labour is not a commodity, simply because the law says so. That is to say, there are statutes and judicial precedents in place that attempt to prevent the commodification of human labour. However, through theoretical approach, the article reveals that labour is akin to the then enslavement of people as labour cannot be separated from one’s self. As a solution to the problem, I propose that workers must have partial ownership of the industries and companies they labour for in order to redress not only the past but the present as well.

item.title: [JLSD] Sexual Violence in Institutions of Higher Learning in South Africa
item.dc:creator: Palesa Lebitse
item.description: In South Africa, labour laws are in place to enact sexual harassment regulations that aim to protect the labour force from sexual harassment and its effects. However, the literature indicates that several factors indicate that sexual harassment or sexual violence at institutions of higher learning, affecting students, differs from the sexual harassment in the workplace. Understanding the act of sexual harassment, the matters of consent, acquaintance rape, reporting and vulnerability due to age are just some of the factors at play in this complex area. There is, however, a lack of substantive research on the prevalence and effect of sexual harassment in non-traditional institutions of higher learning, such as TVHET (formerly FET) colleges, where most previously disadvantaged students pursue their higher education. Whether such institutions have policies in place regarding sexual harassment or sexual violence is largely unknown. This article indicates that even where such policies exist, sexual violence continues. The article explores the responses of these institutions and the national government to sexual violence on campuses being traditionally guided solely by inadequate policies, lacking the potential to deal effectively with this phenomenon. This article then invokes the fundamental rights and values enshrined in the South African Constitution to indicate that the unabated continuance of sexual harassment on these campuses is a failure of the effective accountability of the national government. This is interpreted as the government not exercising its positive duty to enact legislation that protects the human rights and dignity of the victims of such deeds, who are mainly women drawn from the ranks of the previously disadvantaged. This paper argues that the absence of statutory regulation of sexual violence in higher education constitutes a constitutional failure of state accountability. The methodology undertaken for this paper is desktop research and document analysis.

item.title: [JLSD] Examining Gender-Based Violence in the Context of the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence (SODV) Act of 2018 in Eswatini
item.dc:creator: Thembumenzi Ntshalintshali
item.description: Gender-based violence (GBV) remains a major human rights and public health issue in Eswatini. The Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence (SODV) Act of 2018 was an important legislative milestone that attempted to increase legal protections for survivors while also criminalising a wider variety of abuses, such as marital rape and emotional abuse. However, few qualitative studies have looked into how the Act has been implemented. Using a qualitative exploratory design, this study looks into the SODV Act’s implementation and lived experiences. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 40 participants, men and women, including survivors, perpetrators, police officers, social workers, legal professionals, and policymakers. The findings demonstrate a chronic mismatch between legislative aim and practice. While the Act has enhanced legal recognition and reporting methods, structural patriarchy, a lack of public awareness, institutional strengthening, community engagement, and multi-sectoral cooperation remain challenges. The study adds to the literature on legal reform and gender justice in Southern Africa by emphasising implementation issues in socio-cultural and institutional contexts.

item.title: [JLSD] Assessing the Failure of Municipalities in the Free State to Comply with the Obligation to Publish In-Year Budget Monitoring Reports
item.dc:creator: Thabo Khaile
item.description: In-year budget monitoring is widely considered indispensable in ensuring comprehensive and effective budget oversight. However, there is limited empirical evidence available on the extent of compliance with the publication of in-year budget monitoring and performance reports within Free State municipalities. This study examines the extent of compliance with legislative requirements for publishing in-year budget monitoring and performance reports by municipalities in the Free State, South Africa. Using qualitative document analysis supplemented by elements of quantitative content analysis, municipal websites were reviewed to assess whether monthly, quarterly, and mid-year budget monitoring reports were published as required by the Municipal Finance Management Act (MFMA) and related regulations and laws. The findings reveal an alarming pattern of non-compliance, with only 8.7 per cent of municipalities fully compliant, 30.4 per cent partially compliant, and 60.9 per cent failing to publish any required reports. The study highlights that, while the Mangaung Metropolitan Municipality has demonstrated consistent compliance, the majority of local and district municipalities fall short of the minimum statutory requirements. It is concluded that, despite robust legislative frameworks, municipalities in the Free State struggle to meet even the most basic compliance requirements, raising critical concerns about governance, accountability, and the commitment of municipal leadership to constitutional obligations.

item.title: [JLSD] 2024 Control Measures to Curb Violence and Better Regulate Security Services
item.dc:creator: Myrone Stoffels, Juanita M Pienaar, Rene Koraan
item.description: This article discusses the most important developments encompassing legislative measures, case law, and reports dealing with violence and the security services in South Africa in the course of 2024. South Africa remains a violent society, to the extent that crime statistics underscore that violence and crime have generally increased. Gender-based violence has remained prevalent. It is in this light that the Gender-Based Violence and Femicide Act 9 of 2024 is welcomed. Security services remained under scrutiny, with new developments aimed at improving security services on the one hand and decreasing litigation against members on the other. Defence force practices related to the appointment of enquiries into military judges had been found unconstitutional, and basic rights of members enforced. Within the correctional services domain, fundamental rights of inmates relating to access to, respectively, education and food have been reconfirmed. Violent protests and unrest had continued, especially in certain pockets and at specific points in time, while incidents of mass shootings also occurred, including where whole families had been eradicated. Nationwide, communities and families had endured continued violence.
